# Association between Accelerometer-derived Physical Activity-related Metabolic Signature and Stroke: A Cohort Study from UK Biobank

**Authors:** Bowen Tan; Hewanmeng Geng; Zeyu Hao; Zhirong Li; Chengxiang Hu; Tian Yu; Pengyu Wang; Yuanhao Chen; Zhongping Feng; Lina Jin; Baofeng Xu; Rui Liu

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Very Important People (VIP) Unit, China-Japan Union Hospital of Jilin University, Jilin, Changchun, China | bStroke Center, Department of Neurology, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Jilin University, Jilin, Changchun, China | cDepartment of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, School of Public Health, Jilin University, Jilin, Changchun, China | dDepartment of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada

## Abstract

Keywords: Metabolomics, Accelerometer-derived physical activity, Stroke, UK Biobank

## Abstract

Accelerometer-derived physical activity is associated with reduced stroke risk. The biological pathways underpinning this relationship, however, are not yet understood. Herein, we aim to identify metabolic signatures associated with accelerometer-measured PA and investigate their relationships with reduced stroke incidence.

Utilizing UK Biobank accelerometer data, we derived physical activity into total physical activity (TPA), moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and light physical activity (LPA) and linked them to 249 NMR-quantified plasma metabolites. The metabolomic signatures (TPA-/MVPA-/LPA-metabolomic signatures) were developed through internal validation followed by elastic-net regression modeling. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated activity-stroke associations (adjusted for sociodemographic/genetic factors), followed by mediation analysis to quantify metabolomic signature effects.

Through UK Biobank study (N = 29445; 14.1-year follow-up with 513 stroke events), we identified 195 TPA, 173 MVPA, and 164 LPA metabolite associations (FDR < 0.05), with 107, 92, and 15 validated, respectively. Elastic net-derived physical activity-metabolomic signatures (TPA-/MVPA-metabolomic signatures) correlated with physical activity intensities (r = 0.20−0.30, P < 0.001) and were associated with reduced stroke risk: TPA-metabolomic signatures (HR = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.44−0.87); MVPA-metabolomic signatures (HR = 0.50, 95%CI: 0.29−0.88). Mediation analyses showed TPA-metabolomic signatures and MVPA-metabolomic signatures explained 12.2% and 8.5% of physical activity-stroke associations (P < 0.001), implicating specific lipoprotein subclasses and lipids as key mediators.

TPA-metabolomic signatures and MVPA-metabolomic signatures, particularly the 11 key metabolites included, significantly mediate the association between accelerometer-derived physical activity and stroke risk.

## Introduction

Stroke remains a pressing global health challenge. In 2021, the global number of years of healthy life lost due to stroke was 160.4 million, ranking as the fourth leading cause of the global disease burden [1]. This substantial burden underscores the critical importance of strengthening preventive strategies within stroke care systems. Among modifiable lifestyle factors, physical activity represents an effective and accessible preventive approach [2]. Substantial evidence confirms that regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity can reduce stroke risk [3,4]. However, the current body of research has two main limitations: firstly, the questionnaire-based assessment of physical activity constrains the reliability of this evidence [5]; secondly, the biological mechanisms underlying the association between physical activity and stroke risk remain incompletely elucidated [6].

The adoption of accelerometer-based monitoring in large cohorts such as the UK Biobank has enabled a more precise examination of the physical activity-stroke relationship [7]. While establishing a robust exposure-disease association through objective measurement represents significant progress, this constitutes only an initial step. A fundamental question remains inadequately addressed: the biological mechanisms underlying the protective effects of physical activity against stroke [8]. Elucidating these mechanisms not only helps explain the preventive potential of physical activity but also provides key insights to guide and improve the design of prevention strategies [9].

Identifying specific metabolic signatures and plasma metabolites may provide valuable insights into the underlying biological mechanisms [10]. Recent studies have utilized metabolomic profiling to examine how diet and lifestyle influence metabolic function and disease susceptibility, establishing an important foundation for investigating metabolic regulation in the physical activity-stroke relationship [11,12]. Notably, stroke pathogenesis is closely linked to systemic metabolic dysregulation [13]. Adverse lipid profiles and elevated inflammatory markers are well-established contributors to stroke incidence [14,15]. Concurrently, physical activity has been demonstrated to induce beneficial adaptations in numerous metabolites, including those involved in lipid and inflammatory pathways [16]. This convergent evidence leads us to propose a central hypothesis: physical activity-related metabolic signatures and circulating metabolites—particularly those associated with lipid metabolism and inflammation—may mediate the protective effect of physical activity against stroke.

Although previous research has separately examined physical activity-metabolite [16] and metabolite-stroke associations [14], it remains unclear, in large population cohorts, whether there are inter-individual variations in the metabolome in response to accelerometer-measured physical activity, and to what extent such metabolomic variations mediate the association between physical activity and stroke protection [6].

To address this evidence gap, our study leveraged UK Biobank data to develop metabolic signatures associated with accelerometer-measured physical activity and to validate the relationship between these metabolites and incident stroke risk. Most importantly, our research is the first to integrate objective physical activity, plasma metabolomic profiles, and stroke risk within a unified mediation framework, aiming to provide molecular-level evidence for the protective effects of physical activity against stroke.

## Methods

### Study design and population

Recruited between 2006 and 2010, the UKB is a large-scale biomedical database and research resource with detailed genetic and health data on half a million UK participants aged 40–69. Its establishment underwent ethical review and received approval from the National Research Ethics Service Committee North West–Haydock. All individuals in the study provided written informed consent prior to their inclusion. For this analysis, Participants with data on physical activity measured by accelerometers in the UKB were included and participants were excluded based on the following criteria: (1) invalid device calibration or insufficient wear time; (2) prevalent stroke at baseline; (3) missing metabolomics data; and (4) incomplete covariate information [17]. The inclusion flow chart of the study population was illustrated in Fig. 1.

*Fig. 1: Flowchart of the individual selection.*

### Assessment of accelerometer-measured physical activity

The device collected data at a sampling rate of 100 Hz with a dynamic range of ±8 g. Participants wore an Axivity AX3 accelerometer on their dominant wrist continuously for seven days. We extracted individual data from 5-second epoch time series. The study applied four exclusion criteria: insufficient wear time (<72 h), missing hourly data, physiologically implausible accelerations (mean vector magnitude >100 mg), and uncalibrated data. Mean vector magnitude acceleration (mg) served as the primary physical activity metric. We determined the time spent in light physical activity (LPA) and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) using a machine-learning approach, and the total volume of movement behaviors analyzed (TPA, MVPA, LPA) was quantified in minutes per week [17,18]. In this study, the accelerometer-derived physical activity reflects the total volume and intensity of device-measured movement behavior, encompassing bodily movement regardless of its context (e.g., structured exercise, occupational, or household activities). Additional details regarding the definition of accelerometer-measured physical activity were provided in the Supplementary Materials.

### Metabolomic profiling

Between June 2019 and April 2020, we analyzed plasma samples from ∼280,000 UKB participants using NMR spectroscopy (Nightingale Health platform, Finland). This analysis identified 249 metabolites, comprising: (1) 14 lipoprotein subclasses, (2) fatty acids and derivatives, and (3) low-molecular-weight metabolites. For more information on metabolites, see Supplementary Table S1. Systematic and technical variability were minimized through rigorous quality control. This approach facilitated the identification of metabolite signatures linked to accelerometer-measured physical activity and their potential mediating roles in the association between physical activity and stroke risk [19,20]. We employed the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm to impute missing metabolite values, followed by probit transformation to normalize data ranges and reduce distributional skewness [21]. Additional details were summarized in Supplementary Table S1. The missing rates of the metabolites were shown in Supplementary Table S2.

Technical details are available at the following link:

https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/ukb/docs/NMR_companion_phase2.pdf

### Stroke definition

Stroke ascertainment was based on Algorithmically Defined Outcomes (ADOs), which integrate coded data from self-reported conditions, hospital admissions, and death registries using standardized classifications (ICD-9, ICD-10, and UK Biobank-specific codes). ADO validation has been previously established in epidemiological studies [22]. For detailed coding criteria, see Supplementary Materials.

### Assessment and the definition of covariates

The selected sociodemographic features included age at baseline (continuous), sex (male, female), education level [None, CSEs (Certificate of Secondary Education), NVQ (National Vocational Qualification), College, Professional], body mass index (continuous), townsend deprivation index (continuous), hypertension status (yes, no), cardiovascular diseases (yes, no), polygenic risk score for stroke (continuous) [17,23]. In terms of lifestyle habits, smoking, alcohol consumption (continuous), dietary patterns were also considered. Smoking status was categorized as a non-smoker, former smoker, or current smoker based on self-reports. The dietary pattern was determined based on the 7 components used in previous studies, and a healthy dietary pattern was defined as having a score of ≥4 [24].

### Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics included means ± SD for normally distributed continuous variables, medians (range) for skewed continuous variables, and percentages for categorical data.

Participants were randomly assigned to discovery (70 %) and validation (30 %) cohorts. In each cohort, multivariable linear regression was used to estimate the associations of total physical activity (TPA), moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and light physical activity (LPA) with NMR-derived metabolite z-scores [25]. Models were adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, BMI, smoking status, alcohol intake and additional a-priori-defined confounders. A metabolite was carried forward for elastic-net modelling only if (i) the association remained significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple testing (P < 0.05 / number of metabolites tested) and (ii) the regression coefficients for the respective activity parameter displayed concordant directionality in both the discovery and validation sets.

Elastic net analysis was employed to analyze the associations between 249 metabolites and physical activity (TPA/MVPA/LPA). The weight (positive or negative) of each metabolite was assessed according to the regression coefficient of the elastic net regression model. The metabolic signatures were calculated as the weighted sum

of the selected metabolites. For further details regarding the construction of the metabolic signature, please refer to the Supplementary Materials.

physical activity and metabolic signatures were considered as continuous variables. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated SD increments in activity measures and MetS scores with stroke risk, adjusting for sociodemographic, clinical, and genetic factors. No violations of the proportional hazard assumptions were detected through the significance testing of Schoenfeld residuals.

This study employed mediation analysis (using the R "Mediation" package) [26,27] to examine whether "metabolic signatures" mediate the associations between TPA/MVPA/LPA and stroke. The direct effects represent the impact of TPA/MVPA/LPA on stroke independent of the mediator, while the indirect effects reflect the mediating role of metabolic signatures in the relationship between TPA/MVPA/LPA and stroke. Furthermore, we conducted a detailed analysis to elucidate the specific mediating contributions of individual metabolites within the TPA/MVPA/LPA-associated metabolic signatures in the pathway linking physical activity levels to stroke risk.

To examine the robustness of our study, we conducted several sensitivity analyses. To address the potential issue of reverse causation, we performed a sensitivity analysis excluding cases with baseline cardiovascular disease. In addition, we conducted another sensitivity analysis to further investigate the associations between accelerometer-Measured physical activity and its metabolic signature with stroke subtypes, including ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage. All analyses used R 4.4.2.

## Results

### Participant characteristics

This study was based on the UKB, which was divided into a discovery cohort and an internal prospective validation cohort. We included 29445 UKB participants for analysis (Table 1). Participants in the UKB discovery cohort had a mean (SD) age of 56.1 (7.8) years at recruitment, with 55.9% being female. The UKB validation cohort participants had a mean (SD) age of 56.1 (7.8) years at recruitment, with 55.7% being female. The median follow-up time was 14.1 years, during which 513 individuals developed stroke.

### Metabolomic profiles of the accelerometer-derived physical activity

The total volume of physical activity (TPA) was associated with 195 of 249 metabolites (78%) at a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05 (Supplementary Table S3), and 146 metabolites remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Among these 146 associations, 107 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort, including 2 apolipoproteins, 1 cholesterol, 1 cholesterol ester, 6 fatty acids, 1 fluid balance marker, 2 free cholesterols, 1 glycolysis-related metabolite, 1 inflammatory marker, 1 lipid metabolism ratio, 2 lipoprotein particle concentrations, 2 lipoprotein particle sizes, 76 lipoprotein subclasses, 3 other lipids, 3 phospholipids, and 2 triglycerides (Supplementary Table S4).

In the UKB discovery cohort, MVPA was associated with 173 of 249 metabolites (69%) at a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05, and 125 metabolites remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Among these 125 associations, 92 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort, including 65 lipoprotein subclasses, 2 apolipoproteins, 1 cholesterol, 1 cholesteryl ester, 5 fatty acids, 1 free cholesterol, 1 inflammatory marker, 1 lipid metabolite ratio, 2 lipoprotein particle concentrations, 2 lipoprotein particle sizes, 1 phospholipid, 3 other lipids, 5 total lipids, and 2 triglycerides. Light-intensity physical activity was associated with 164 of 249 metabolites (66%) at FDR < 0.05, with 90 metabolites remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Of these 90 associations, 15 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort. Further details regarding the discovery and validation sets were provided in Supplementary Tables S4, S5 and Fig. 2(A). We employed the elastic net model as a dimensionality reduction method to regress metabolites against total volume of physical activity, MVPA, and LPA, thereby constructing an accelerometer-derived physical activity metabolomic signature score (PA-MetS) (Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2). Taking TPA-MetS as an example, 32 metabolites were selected from the 249 for TPA-MetS construction (Supplementary Table S5). Positive weights were assigned to triglycerides in small HDL, triglycerides in very large VLDL, and free cholesterol in small HDL, while negative weights were assigned to creatinine, lactate, and glycoprotein acetyls. Details on the weights of MVPA-MetS and LPA-MetS were provided in Supplementary Tables S6, S7 and Fig. 2(B). TPA-MetS showed significant correlation with TPA (Pearson’s r = 0.30, P < 0.001 in the UKB internal validation cohort; Supplementary Figs. S1), as did MVPA-MetS with MVPA (r = 0.20, P < 0.001) and LPA-MetS with LPA (r = 0.23, P < 0.001) in the same cohort (Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3).

*Fig. 2: (A) Heatmap of metabolite associations with accelerometer-derived physical activity (TPA, MVPA, LPA). (B) The weights of the metabolites selected in the PA‐MetS.*

### Accelerometer-derived physical activity metabolomic signature and stroke outcomes

We evaluated the associations of physical activity and PA-MetS with stroke in the UKB. Both TPA, MVPA, TPA-MetS, and MVPA-MetS were significantly associated with lower stroke risk. For instance, each standard deviation (SD) increase in TPA and TPA-MetS yielded hazard ratios (HRs) of 0.98 (95% CI: 0.97, 0.99; P = 0.003) and 0.61 (95% CI:0.44, 0.87; P = 0.005), respectively (Table 2). However, no significant associations were observed for LPA or LPA-MetS, with HRs per SD increase of 0.99 (95% CI: 0.99, 1.00; P = 0.063) for LPA and 0.57 (95% CI: 0.32, 1.01; P = 0.056) for LPA-MetS.

Mediation analysis revealed that 12.2% of the association between TPA and incident stroke was mediated by TPA-MetS (P for mediation < 0.001) (Fig. 3B), while 8.50% of the MVPA-stroke association was mediated by MVPA-MetS (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3A). Additionally, analysis of metabolite contributions to the metabolic signatures identified multiple mediators, such as xxl-VLDL-L and s-HDL-TG for MVPA and TPA, respectively (Supplementary Table S8). To address reverse causation, sensitivity analyses excluding baseline cardiovascular disease cases yielded consistent findings: MVPA-MetS and TPA-MetS showed mediation effects of 4.48% and 14.33%, respectively (see details in Tables S9-S13 and Supplementary Fig. S4). ## Discussion

In this prospective cohort, higher levels of accelerometer-measured MVPA and TPA showed significant inverse correlations with stroke risk, consistent with previous findings [4]. We have identified 32 TPA-related metabolites, 11 MVPA-related metabolites, and 5 LPA-related metabolites. Building on these results, we developed TPA-MetS, MVPA-MetS, and LPA-MetS to comprehensively assess how physical activity-associated metabolomic patterns mediate the physical activity-stroke association, while also elucidating individual metabolites' contributions within these signatures. Mediation analyses demonstrate that both TPA and MVPA-associated metabolomic signatures significantly attenuated stroke risk through distinct mechanisms. Single-mediator analyses further revealed that TPA primarily conferred protection via modulation of lipoprotein interactions and fatty acid metabolism, whereas MVPA specifically targeted very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) metabolic pathways.

Our results revealed the stroke-preventive potential of TPA and MVPA, along with their underlying metabolic regulatory mechanisms. Notably, the integrated metabolomic signatures demonstrated significantly better explanatory power for stroke risk than individual metabolites, highlighting the systemic advantages of metabolic network regulation.

The functional significance of these metabolomic signatures aligns with fundamental principles of metabolic regulation. Metabolites serve not merely as biochemical endpoints but as crucial regulatory molecules bridging environmental exposures and cellular physiological states [9]. Their dynamic changes reflect the organism's adaptive responses to external stimuli and form molecular connections between exposures and phenotypic outcomes [10]. The construction of metabolic signatures not only facilitates the exploration of the link between physical activity and stroke, but also reveals potential common metabolic responses of the body to physical activity [9]. However, the heterogeneity in metabolic responses among individuals exposed to the same level of physical activity should not be overlooked [28]. Metabolites identified through the development of such metabolic signatures may serve as potential biomarkers reflecting physical activity responses [29]. Monitoring these biomarkers during physical activity could help identify individuals who do not exhibit beneficial metabolic changes following appropriate levels of exercise prior to the onset of stroke, allowing for timely adjustments to prevention strategies [28].

Our findings are consistent with previous research on physical activity-induced metabolic effects, such as the Finnish Twin Cohort Study demonstrating that sustained physical activity promotes conversion of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids while reducing VLDL concentrations [16]. Given the established roles of inflammation and oxidative stress in stroke pathogenesis, our observation that both TPA and MVPA signatures include glycoprotein acetylation (an inflammatory marker) supports the hypothesis that physical activity mitigates these pathological processes through multiple pathways. This observation aligns with established mechanisms whereby physical activity promotes Nrf2 nuclear translocation and downstream activation of antioxidant gene expression [30]. The apolipoprotein B/apolipoprotein A-I (apoB/apo A-I) ratio demonstrates superior predictive value compared to traditional lipid parameters [31]. Studies have demonstrated that physical activity reduces apoB levels through decreasing visceral adipose tissue, consequently leading to a lower apoB/apo A-I ratio [32].

Different Physical activity intensity appears to induce distinct metabolic effects [9,33]. Animal studies had shown that moderate-intensity exercised activates ventromedial hypothalamic (VMH) noradrenergic neurons to enhance white adipose tissue fatty acid oxidation [34], while high-intensity could exercise modulates gut microbiota to reduce inflammatory cytokines [35]. Clinical evidence also corroborated our findings: A cross-sectional study demonstrated MVPA's (but not LPA's) important role in reducing VLDL particle concentration and size, particularly in populations with cardiovascular risk factors [36]. A case-control study reported significantly improved lipid profiles, including reduced TC, increased HDL-C, and lowered atherogenic indices, in high-intensity physical activity groups [37]. This finding is consistent with our observed MVPA-specific regulation of lipoprotein metabolism. Although we have identified LPA-associated metabolic signatures, their lack of direct association with stroke risk suggests that MVPA may offer more definitive preventive benefits. This aligns with existing evidence that regular MVPA not only reduces stroke risk but also ameliorates key risk factors like hypertension and diabetes [3,38].

Although the metabolites incorporated into the metabolomic signatures were generally consistent with previous studies [6], We systematically assessed mediation by both metabolomic signatures and its constituent metabolites, quantifying how distinct levels of physical activity confer stroke protection. Mediation analysis of metabolomic signatures components revealed that lipoprotein subclasses mediated effects for both TPA and MVPA, while omega-6 fatty acid proportions specifically mediated TPA effects. The strongest mediators were cholesteryl esters to total lipids in l-HDL, triglycerides in s-HDL, and omega-6 fatty acids to total fatty acids ratio.Prior research indicates HDL cholesterol esterification plays a vital role in reverse cholesterol transport and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prevention [39]. This explains the significant mediating effect of elevated cholesteryl ester proportion in HDL on reduced stroke risk observed in our study. In our study, TPA demonstrated an inverse correlation with small HDL triglyceride (HDL-TG) levels. Previous research has demonstrated that increased levels of small HDL-TG can impair HDL function and are correlated with metabolic disturbances, including hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, as well as cardiovascular risks like carotid plaque formation [40].

In sensitivity analyses stratified by stroke etiology, the inverse associations of both TPA- and MVPA-related metabolomic signatures with stroke risk were predominantly observed for ischemic stroke, while no significant associations were detected for hemorrhagic subtypes. This finding suggests that the protective associations of physical activity-related metabolomic features are stronger for ischemic stroke than for hemorrhagic stroke, indicating that these signatures primarily reflect pathways related to atherosclerosis and metabolic mechanisms, such as improved lipid metabolism and reduced inflammation [41,42]. In contrast, hemorrhagic stroke is more influenced by vascular fragility and hypertension-related processes [43], which are less represented in physical activity-induced metabolic alterations. Future studies integrating metabolomics, proteomics, and vascular imaging data are warranted to elucidate these subtype-specific mechanisms.

This study has several strengths. First, the large-scale cohort with high-quality metabolomics and precisely measured physical activity ensured robust findings. Second, we provided the first comprehensive metabolomic characterization of physical activity's biological mechanisms in stroke prevention, with quantitative comparison of protective effects across the volume of physical activity through mediation analyses.

However, this study has certain limitations that should be acknowledged. First, notwithstanding the prospective design, multivariable adjustments, and mediation analyses employed to bolster the robustness of our causal inference, the possibility of residual confounding cannot be entirely ruled out. These methodological strengths remain insufficient to establish causality. Future studies are warranted to confirm a causal relationship. Second, the mediation analysis employed a simplified model of potential pathways through which physical activity may influence stroke occurrence, and future studies should investigate additional mediating factors. Third, the study population was exclusively drawn from the United Kingdom; Future research should evaluate the generalizability of these findings to different populations. Fourth, although the accelerometer provides an objective measure of the volume and intensity of physical activity, it cannot distinguish the context or purpose of the movement (e.g., structured exercise versus occupational activity). Finally, the metabolic effects of physical activity exhibit notable temporal specificity. Our study did not analyze levels of physical activity in specific time windows; future research could explore how the chronobiology of physical activity (e.g., time of day) influences metabolic profiles.

## Conclusion

Our study elucidated the metabolomic mechanisms underlying the inverse association between physical activity and stroke risk. We identified distinct metabolic signatures (TPA-MetS, MVPA-MetS) reflecting levels of physical activity. Key mediators included lipoprotein subclasses and fatty acids, highlighting the role of lipid metabolism and inflammation in stroke prevention. Our findings advanced the understanding of physical activity's protective effects by linking objective activity metrics to systemic metabolic reprogramming, offering novel biomarkers for precision prevention and interventions.
